description: Site-specific archaeology, dated botanical finds, analytical markers, ancient testimony, interpretation disputes, and explicit limits. No new phytocannabinoid canon or clinical claims.
editorial_notice: Curated foundational sources and critical reporting, not a systematic archaeology review. Methodologic uncertainty and independent critique are first-class records.
medical_boundary: Ancient ritual or presumed medicinal use does not establish medical efficacy or safety. Archaeological evidence cannot justify replacing clinical care.

sources.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2,800 years ago
sources.note: Science, 5 Nov 2026; Tunnug 1 seeds and ancient hair chemistry. Check the original analytical methods and supplements before concluding consumption.

sources.title: Cannabis was used as an intoxicant as early as 2,800 years ago
sources.note: Source for early eighth-century BCE direct seed dating, reported CBN-like hair signals, weak putative THC, and explicit limits on route, dose, and cultivation.

sources.title: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high, 2,800 years ago, study suggests
sources.authors: Keaten J and Jenne P, Associated Press
sources.note: Quotes independent forensic toxicologist Volker Auwärter questioning the strength of hair analysis and inability to exclude external exposure; critique is not a published refutation.

sources.title: The origins of cannabis smoking: Chemical residue evidence from the first millennium BCE in the Pamirs
sources.note: Science Advances study of Jirzankal GC-MS braziers and burnt stones. Introduction contextualizes older Pazyryk archaeology and cautions that other historical cannabis finds can be poorly verified.

sources.title: Histories, Book IV, sections 73–75
sources.note: Fifth-century BCE textual report about Scythian post-burial purification using hemp and hot stones; ancient narrative is not a chemically verified Pazyryk excavation record.

claims.title: Directly dated cannabis seeds at Tunnug 1
claims.summary: Approximately one thousand cannabis seeds were recovered from an elite funerary context; six seeds underwent radiocarbon dating consistent with the early eighth century BCE.
claims.model: Excavated funerary mound; preserved botanical specimens
claims.boundary: Seeds demonstrate botanical presence and mortuary deposition, not route of administration, intoxicating potency, cultivation, or medicinal use.

claims.title: Hair signals consistent with CBN and weaker possible THC
claims.summary: The study reports high-resolution mass-spectrometric signals in ancient hair consistent with cannabinol (CBN) and weaker mass-consistent signals for THC.
claims.model: Preserved hair from Tunnug 1 central burial chamber
claims.boundary: Reported signals require analytical scrutiny. A CBN-associated signal is not proof of the quantity or route of consumption, impairment, or intentional intoxication.

claims.title: Consumption inference is actively disputed
claims.summary: Study authors interpret the co-occurrence of seeds and hair signatures as evidence of psychoactive cannabis use. An independent forensic toxicologist argues that the hair analysis does not adequately exclude external exposure.
claims.model: Scientific interpretation of ancient hair biomarkers
claims.boundary: Treat intentional ingestion/inhalation as a hypothesis supported by authors but contested, not as an observed event. No demonstrated sedative use before sacrifice.

claims.title: CBN on wooden braziers and burned stones
claims.summary: Ren et al. identified chemical markers of cannabis, including CBN, in charred interior residues from wooden braziers and on some burnt stones. Exterior vessel samples were negative controls.
claims.model: Mortuary vessels and heated stones, approximately 500 BCE
claims.boundary: Ancient residue CBN detection supports cannabis burning but does not directly recover ancient THC concentrations, human dose, or individual subjective effects.

claims.title: Funerary inhalation is plausible at Jirzankal
claims.summary: Cannabis residues on vessels in a mortuary context support researchers' interpretation that plants were burned for ritualized inhalation.
claims.boundary: No observed individual inhalation, exact method, standardized potency, or medicinal clinical efficacy can be reconstructed.

claims.title: Pazyryk kurgan 2 contained hemp-burning apparatus
claims.summary: Published archaeological accounts reviewed in Ren et al. describe a small wooden tent frame, copper containers with heat-affected stones, carbonized hemp seeds, and a leather seed pouch at Pazyryk kurgan 2.
claims.model: Specific elite burial at Pazyryk kurgan 2
claims.boundary: This is not evidence that almost all burials contained personal smoking kits; identify the specific kurgan and distinguish old reports from modern residue chemistry.

claims.title: Herodotus described hemp fumes in post-burial purification
claims.summary: Histories IV.73–75 describes Scythians using heated stones and hemp in a felt-covered structure after burial and responding joyfully.
claims.model: Fifth-century BCE Greek narrative about Scythians
claims.boundary: The text is a historically situated account, not a direct record of chemical testing or proof that the same practice occurred at every Pazyryk burial.

claims.title: Do not confuse separate Pazyryk burials or infer cancer treatment
claims.summary: Evidence for cannabis-burning equipment at specific Pazyryk graves should not be attributed without verification to the Ukok Ice Maiden or treated as evidence of a cancer therapy.
claims.model: Comparison of separately excavated Pazyryk-era burials
claims.boundary: No source in this dataset establishes cannabis in the Ice Maiden's own burial or that cannabis was medically administered for breast cancer. Cancer findings do not prove treatment.

claims.title: Ancient cannabis findings are not modern therapeutic trials
claims.summary: Archaeological artifacts, molecular traces, and ancient written accounts document historical contexts and sometimes chemical signatures, not controlled evidence of health outcomes.
claims.model: Historical archaeology compared with modern clinical evidence
claims.boundary: Historical use does not establish clinical efficacy, safety, dosage, medical indication, or spiritual universality.
